description: We are Analog Space Mission Explorers
summary:
SPACE ANALOG-360: Earth Analog Discovery for Moon and Mars Exploration

SPACE ANALOG-360 is an interactive planetary research prototype developed to identify Earth environments that resemble selected locations on the Moon and Mars. The application allows users to explore Earth locations using an interactive globe, view photographs, examine geographical coordinates, and compare environmental characteristics.
The project addresses the NASA challenge by comparing six key features: geology, temperature, water and ice, dust and wind, terrain, and subsurface conditions. It investigates potential Earth analogs such as the Bodélé Depression in Chad, Makgadikgadi Pans in Botswana, the Deccan Traps in India, and Spiti Valley in India.
This project is important because Earth-based environments can help scientists test exploration technologies, study geological processes, and prepare astronauts and robotic systems for future planetary missions. SPACE ANALOG-360 aims to make the discovery of potential planetary analog locations easier, more visual, and more accessible. Its future development will focus on integrating verified NASA and scientific datasets to improve the accuracy of its comparisons and rankings.
details:
SPACE ANALOG-360: Earth Analog Discovery for Moon and Mars Exploration

SPACE ANALOG-360 is an interactive web-based research prototype designed to identify potential locations on Earth that share geological and environmental characteristics with selected regions of the Moon and Mars. Users can select planetary reference locations, such as Jezero Crater on Mars or Shackleton Crater on the Moon, and explore potential Earth analogs using an interactive 3D globe, labeled locations, photographs, geographical coordinates, and environmental information.

The application uses a comparison framework based on six important factors: geology, temperature, water and ice, dust and wind, terrain, and subsurface conditions. It features potential analog locations such as the Bodélé Depression in Chad, Makgadikgadi Pans in Botswana, the Deccan Traps in India, and Spiti Valley in India.

The project benefits planetary research and education by helping users understand how Earth's natural environments can support preparation for future space exploration. These environments could provide opportunities to study geological processes, test rover mobility, investigate dust movement, and evaluate exploration technologies before they are used on the Moon or Mars.

Our intended impact is to encourage the discovery of new Earth locations that could support planetary science experiments, rather than focusing only on already established analog sites. We hope to develop the platform further by integrating verified NASA, USGS, satellite, geological, and climate datasets.
